label: July–August 1881
atlas_dek: The episodes reported in July and August 1881 from our dossiers: lynchings of any race and anti-Black violence, placed on 1910 county lines and by month (some June events were first reported in July). Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 92 episodes reported in July and August 1881. These two months cover two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white, Mexican and Chinese victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are therefore included here, unlike in our other months. The episodes come from the located events in the July and August 1881 tables, which include June events first reported in July; from the Monroe Work Today inventory, our only lynching list for this year (three lynchings our first search missed: the “Black Kid” at Silverton, Colorado, Spence near Frog Level, Louisiana, and the ambush of Mexican traders at Las Animas); and from a check of every article for attacks by one person. We did not write dossiers for seven events that were plainly out of scope from the table alone: a duplicate record, a lawful whipping at Alexandria, a rescue at Lake City, white patrolmen resigning at Philadelphia, a Black detective striking a Black woman at Chicago, the assassination of an Arkansas editor with no race given, and a manhunt near Camden, South Carolina, in which no one was hurt. Searches covered each month’s papers, plus the next month’s for more on known episodes. For 1881 the search used white papers only.

Fourteen of the 106 dossiers are set aside. Four are duplicates folded into another record: the “Petersburg, Tennessee” report, which is the Dyersburg lynching of Mike Wells; George Absner at Abbeville, Louisiana, who is William Epperson; a second record of the attempt on Frank Hudson; and the Heard County, Georgia, report of the Waldrop lynching. Four belong to other months: the attempt at the Grand Haven, Michigan, jail and the killings of Dick Wood and Bob Dill in June, and the February lynching at Springfield, Tennessee, known only from the governor’s reward. The hangings at New Madrid, Missouri, were a legal execution; the “lynching” at Hilliard, Wyoming, was a staged joke on train passengers; the Tucson lynching was a wire supposition the local paper rejected; Bill Sims, at Pinckney’s Landing, Arkansas, shot a justice and escaped unharmed; no report gives the race of Rhodes and Crowder, shot in their Florida camp by unknown men; and the cabin-court story of Dick Marsh is an undated frontier sketch.

The ambush of Mexican traders at Las Animas is kept to show a difference with the inventory: Monroe Work Today lists thirteen Mexican victims of a reprisal near Fronteras, while the 1881 papers place a robbery ambush in Sonora with four or five men supposed killed. It is outside the United States and not counted.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights (the shooting at a Black ball on False River, Louisiana; a Fourth of July brawl in Baltimore) and threats with no force (white railroad laborers’ protest against Black workers at Middletown, New York) stay in the reader but out of the totals. Peonage, force used to hold a Black worker to labor, is always included; a search of July and August papers found no case.

Attacks by one person: our definition covers violence by groups and by people acting with public authority, so an attack by a single private person is normally left out. A check of every July and August article for such attacks added seven, kept and marked as one-person attacks: killings and assaults of Black men at Baltimore, Grand Haven, Nashville, Covington (Tennessee) and Ruckersville (Georgia) in August, and in July the whipping of a Black boy at Haynesville, Louisiana, and a knife attack on a Black bootblack in Washington. The same check found the fight on Edisto Island, South Carolina, in which two white brothers beat Wilson Calder, who died the next day; it is a group event and counted as one.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: no entry has had human review.
